sections.body:
Mental arithmetic is doing a calculation in your head, without a calculator and without paper. It is a working method, not a party trick. The method matters more than the speed, because a fast wrong number costs more time than a slow right one: the wrong number gets used.

There are two different skills here. **Speed** is how long you take. **Accuracy** is whether the number you say is true. They are not the same skill, and a person can have one without the other. Some people multiply small numbers very fast and lose a digit in the middle. Others work carefully, more slowly, and are right every time.

A second mistake is to treat a guess as an answer. A guess that sounds confident is worse than an honest pause, because the listener cannot tell that the number was never checked. A checked answer can always be defended: you can show the rough size of the answer, the shortcut you used, or the reverse check.

So the honest line is simple: **give me a moment to work that out**. Nobody expects a number on the first syllable. What they expect is a number that is right. Every shortcut in this article comes with a way to check it, and a shortcut without a check is only a way to be wrong faster.
examples: Mental arithmetic is a method, not a speed test.
Give me a moment to work that out; I will give you the number I can check.
A wrong number costs more time than a slow right one.
sections.heading: Fast is not the same as right

terms.example: Mental arithmetic gave me the rough figure, and the check gave me the right one.
terms.gloss: Doing a calculation in your head, without a calculator and without paper.

sections.body:
The most useful shortcut for multiplication is **round and adjust**. You round one factor to a friendly value, multiply the easy version, and then correct the result by the amount you rounded. The correction is small, and the easy part is genuinely easy. Friendly values are the ones you can multiply without thinking: 10, 20, 25, 50, 100 and their halves. A factor that ends in 1 or 9 usually sits close to one of them, so 19 is treated as 20 and 98 as 100.

Now work the product 19 × 24. Round 19 to 20 and multiply: 20 × 24 = 480. You added 1 to the first factor, so you must remove one lot of 24 from the result: 480 − 24 = 456. The answer is 456. You can confirm it in one line: 19 × 24 = 456.

The method works in both directions. For 18 × 24, round 18 up to 20 and subtract two lots of 24: 480 − 48 = 432. For 21 × 24, round down to 20 and add one lot of 24: 480 + 24 = 504.

Two rules keep the method honest. Round **one** factor, not both. And the correction must use the factor you did not round: here you changed the first factor by 1, so you add or subtract 1 × 24, which is 24 and not 19.
examples: I rounded 19 up to 20 and subtracted one lot of 24, so 19 × 24 = 456.
Round one factor only, and correct with the factor you did not round.
The correction is one times 24, so I take away 24 and not 19.
sections.heading: Round and adjust: one worked product
steps: Choose the factor to round and the friendly value to round it to: 19 becomes 20.
Note the size of the change you made: you added 1 to the first factor.
Correct the result by the change times the other factor: 480 − (1 × 24) = 456.
Say the answer with its unit: 456 items.

sections.body:
Every shortcut in the list has the same shape: you change the number to an easier one, you do the easy part, and you put back exactly what you changed. A shortcut with no easy undo is a guess, not a method.

Two of the rows carry most of the work. **Round and adjust** handles any product with a factor near a friendly value. **Split a product** handles a product of two two-digit numbers: you break one of them into tens and units, and you add two smaller products.

The two percentage rows use one fact: 10 % is one tenth, so 10 % of a number is found by dividing by ten, and 5 % is half of that. A percentage taken as a fraction of ten is often the fastest way to work out a discount, a tax or a margin.

The last row, **double and halve**, is the old way of removing a factor of 4. Halve one factor and double the other, and the product does not change.
examples: 15 % of 240 is 24 plus 12, so 36.
sections.heading: Eight shortcuts that never lie

rows: Move the decimal point one or two places to the right.
Round one factor to a friendly value, then add or subtract the change.
Break one factor into tens and units, and add the two smaller products.
Break both factors into tens and units, multiply the four parts, and add them.
Subtract from the next round number, then take away the complement: 100 − 35 = 65, and 100 − 78 = 22.
A percentage as a fraction of ten
10 % is one tenth, so find the tenth and double it for 20 %.
Take 10 % and add half of it for the other 5 %.
Halve one factor and double the other; the product stays the same.

sections.body:
Estimate is a rough number, close enough to show whether a real answer is possible. **Rounding** is writing a number as the nearest convenient value, usually the nearest ten, hundred or thousand: 47 rounds to 50, and 42 rounds to 40.

Compensation is the correction you make after you have rounded a number. **Carry** is the tens you pass into the next column when the digits of one column add up to ten or more: in 8 + 7 you write 5 and carry 1.

Remainder is the part that is left over when one number does not divide into the other. **Quotient** is the result of the division without that leftover part: 87 divided by 7 gives the quotient 12 and the remainder 3.

Digit sum is the total of all the digits of a number. A number is a multiple of 9 exactly when its digit sum is a multiple of 9: the digit sum of 1296 is 1 + 2 + 9 + 6 = 18, and 18 is a multiple of 9.
examples: My estimate was about 1,500, and the exact answer was 1,296.
47 rounds to 50, and I add the compensation back.
87 divided by 7 gives the quotient 12 and the remainder 3.
The digit sum of 1296 is 18, so it is a multiple of 9.

sections.body:
A shortcut without a check is a fast way to be wrong. Four checks cost seconds and catch almost every slip: the size of the answer, the operation in reverse, the digit sum, and the unit. The first one is the quickest: **check the size**. Round each number to an easy value and work the rough product: about 50 times about 30 is about 1500. If your answer is 15 or 15000, it is wrong before you check it any further. An estimate catches the mistakes of size, and it never catches a small slip in the last step.

Do the operation in reverse. Addition and subtraction undo each other, and so do multiplication and division. If you divided 87 by 7 and got the quotient 12 with a remainder of 3, multiply back: 12 × 7 = 84, and 84 + 3 = 87. If your answer had been 13, then 13 × 7 = 91, which is already too big. **Use the digit sum for multiples of 9.** A number is a multiple of 9 exactly when its digit sum is a multiple of 9. So if both factors are multiples of 3, the product must be a multiple of 9 as well.

Check the unit and the order of magnitude. The answer to 48 crates of 27 bottles is a number of bottles, not crates, and not bottles per crate. If the question asks for a length and your answer carries no unit, it is not finished.

Here is a slip being caught. You need the number of bottles in 48 crates of 27 bottles. You work 48 × 30 = 1440, then subtract 48 × 3 = 144, and you get 1296. The size check agrees: about 1500 is near 1296. Now suppose the subtraction slips and you write 1298. The reverse check catches it, because 1298 ÷ 48 is not a whole number of crates. The digit sum catches it as well: the digit sum of 1298 is 1 + 2 + 9 + 8 = 20, which is not a multiple of 9, while 48 and 27 are both multiples of 3, so the product has to be a multiple of 9. The right answer is 1296, and its digit sum is 18.
examples: About 50 times about 30 is about 1,500, so 1,296 is the right size.
Multiply the quotient back and add the remainder; you must get the number you started with.
I check the unit before I check the digits: the answer is bottles, not crates.
sections.heading: Check the answer you did in your head
steps: Estimate the size of the answer from the rounded numbers: about 1,500 bottles.
Do the operation in reverse and check that you get the number you started with.
Test the digit sum when the factors are multiples of 3: 1 + 2 + 9 + 6 = 18.
Say the answer with its unit: 1,296 bottles in 48 crates.
If any check fails, do the calculation again instead of adjusting the number you like.

sections.body:
There is a professional way to buy time. When a number is needed and you do not have it yet, say what you are doing: **"Let me work that out."** It is one second of speech, and it buys the three seconds the calculation needs.

Other honest sentences: **"I will check that and come back to you."** **"That is roughly 1,300; the exact figure is 1,296."** **"I do not have that number with me."** Each one says what you know and what you do not know, without pretending.

What not to do: do not say a number you have not checked, only because the silence feels long. A number said with confidence is taken as checked. If it is wrong, it is used, and the correction has to travel back through everyone who used it.

A checked answer beats a fast wrong one every time. The checked answer survives the meeting, the report and the shift handover. The fast wrong number has to be caught later, usually by somebody else, and it costs that person the same work you avoided.
examples: Let me work that out.
That is roughly 1,300; the exact figure is 1,296.
I will check that and come back to you.
I do not have that number with me, but it is close to 1,300.
sections.heading: The honest sentences at work

sections.body:
Say the rough size first, then the exact number. "About 1,300 bottles, and exactly 1,296." The size takes one second and gives the listener something to test the number against. If the two disagree, you have found the error before anybody used the number.

Keep the size in the same unit as the answer. A size in metres and an answer in centimetres cannot check each other.

Say it out loud. A number you only think about is a number you check only sometimes.
examples: About 1,300 bottles, and exactly 1,296.
Say the size in the same unit as the answer, or the check will not catch anything.
I have a rough figure of 1,300, and I am checking it against the count.
sections.heading: Give the size before the number

sections.body:
These are the sentences that make a number sound checked, whether you worked it out in your head or on paper. The pattern is the same in all of them: the size, the exact number, and the way you got it.

Use the size first and the exact number after it. Keep the way you got it short: "I rounded 19 to 20 and subtracted one lot of 24, so 19 × 24 = 456" is enough. When the check itself is worth saying, say it in one line: "the digit sum is 18, a multiple of 9, so the answer can be right." And "Let me work that out" is always better than a number you did not check.
examples: Let me work that out; give me a second.
That is about 1,300; the exact figure is 1,296.
87 divided by 7 is 12 with a remainder of 3.
15 % of 800 is 80 plus 40, which is 120.
sections.heading: Sentences you can reuse

item.summary: Fast mental arithmetic is a set of honest shortcuts, and every shortcut needs a check. After reading this article you can round and adjust a product, split a product into parts, work in tens, take a percentage as a fraction of ten, and subtract with a complement. You can also estimate an answer before you give it and check the answer in reverse.
item.title: Fast Mental Arithmetic You Can Check
